title: The Critical Rendering Path
summary: DOM plus CSSOM becomes pixels through render tree, layout, paint, and composite — and knowing exactly where a resource blocks that pipeline is what separates a real performance fix from a guess.

slides.markdown:
Once the DOM and CSSOM exist (covered in `dom-and-cssom`), the browser still has real work to do before anything appears on screen: combine the two trees, figure out where every element sits and how big it is, fill in pixels, then assemble the final frame — often with GPU help.

This pipeline is the **critical rendering path**, and "how would you make this page paint faster" is one of the most common frontend performance questions, precisely because the answer depends on knowing which stage is actually the bottleneck.

This topic walks render tree construction, layout, paint, and compositing, then the resources that block each stage — and closes with how to actually answer the speed-up question instead of reciting "minify your JS."

The **render tree** is what you get when the DOM and CSSOM are combined — but it isn't a straight merge. Only elements that will actually be **painted** make it in.

Two categories are excluded entirely: elements with `display: none` (and their subtree), and non-visual elements like `<head>`, `<script>`, `<meta>`. Note the distinction from `visibility: hidden` — that element still occupies layout space and is still in the render tree, just not painted; `display: none` removes it from the tree altogether, which is why toggling `display` is more expensive to animate than toggling `visibility` or `opacity`.

Each render tree node carries the DOM node's identity plus its final, cascaded CSSOM styles — this is the structure layout will actually operate on next.

slides.subTitle: Also called reflow
slides.markdown:
**Layout** walks the render tree and computes the exact box for every node: x/y position and width/height, in device pixels, accounting for the box model, flexbox/grid rules, and the viewport size.

This is inherently a **global-ish** operation — changing one element's width can shift every sibling and descendant after it (a table column resizing pushes everything in that column down the page). That's why layout is comparatively expensive: it isn't "recompute one box," it's "recompute however much of the tree that one change invalidates," which in the worst case is the whole document.

This is also the stage most people mean when they say "reflow" — the term predates "layout" but describes the same computation.

**Paint** takes the render tree, now with exact geometry from layout, and produces actual pixels: fills, borders, text, shadows, images — for every visible element, typically split across multiple **layers**.

Paint is usually cheaper than layout per pixel, but it isn't free, and "paint" is deceptively broad — a `box-shadow` or `border-radius` on many elements can dominate paint time because each is a nontrivial rasterization operation, not a simple fill.

DevTools' Rendering tab has a literal "Paint flashing" overlay that highlights repainted regions in green as they happen — turning it on while interacting with your own UI is the fastest way to discover you're repainting far more of the screen than you think you are.

slides.sectionTitle: Compositing — assembling layers with the GPU
slides.markdown:
Some elements get promoted to their **own layer** — a separately-painted bitmap the GPU can move, scale, or fade independently, without re-running layout or paint on the rest of the page. `transform`, `opacity`, `will-change`, and video/canvas elements commonly trigger this.

The payoff: animating a layer's `transform` only requires the **compositor thread** to recombine already-painted layers into a new frame — no main-thread layout, no repaint. That's the entire reason "animate transform/opacity, not top/left/width" is repeated so often: the former can skip straight to compositing, the latter forces the full layout → paint → composite chain on every single frame.

The catch: too many layers cost real GPU memory (each is a full bitmap), so promoting everything with blanket `will-change: transform` can trade a CPU bottleneck for a GPU one.

End to end: DOM + CSSOM → **render tree** → **layout** (geometry) → **paint** (pixels per layer) → **composite** (GPU assembles final frame).

A given change doesn't always walk the whole chain — that's the key optimization insight. A `transform` change can skip straight to composite. A color change skips layout but still needs paint. A width or `display` change forces the full sequence, layout included. Knowing which category your change falls into is what "which CSS properties are expensive to animate" is really asking.

slides.markdown:
Two resource types are **render-blocking** by default, meaning the browser won't produce the first frame until they're resolved:

- **CSS in `<head>`** — because the CSSOM must be complete before styles can be resolved for anything, and the render tree can't be built without it.
- **Synchronous `<script>` tags** — because they can mutate the DOM the parser is still building (see `dom-and-cssom`), so parsing halts, which delays everything downstream of it too, including layout.

A render-blocking stylesheet linked in `<head>` is standard and usually correct — you want styled content, not a flash of unstyled markup. The problem case is a **large** stylesheet blocking on styles the user won't see for several screens, which is exactly what critical CSS extraction targets.

Two established techniques directly target the render-blocking resources above:

- **Critical CSS** — inline the small subset of CSS needed for above-the-fold content directly in `<head>` (so first paint doesn't wait on a network round trip for the full stylesheet), and load the rest asynchronously via `<link rel="preload" as="style" onload="...">` or a similar pattern.
- **Deferring non-critical JS** — `defer` (or moving scripts to the end of `<body>`) so parsing and the render tree aren't held up by script execution that doesn't affect the first frame.

The production numbers are real: inlining critical CSS commonly improves First Contentful Paint by several hundred milliseconds on a slow connection, because it removes one full round trip from the critical path before any pixel can appear.

slides.sectionTitle: A late <link> or injected CSS-in-JS silently re-triggering layout
slides.markdown:
A `<link rel="stylesheet">` placed in `<body>` (not `<head>`) still works, but it's a common trap: everything the browser already laid out and painted **before** that link finishes loading can get its styles changed retroactively, forcing a full layout and repaint of already-rendered content — a visible flash or shift, not just a performance cost.

Runtime CSS-in-JS libraries can cause the identical problem: injecting a `<style>` tag after initial render (common with libraries that compute styles from props on mount) forces the same late recalculation. This is one of the concrete causes behind unexplained **Cumulative Layout Shift** regressions in Core Web Vitals — a style injected a beat after first paint moves content that a user may have already started interacting with.

The fix is the same one CSS-in-JS libraries eventually adopt: extract styles at build time or inject them before first paint, not after.

Rough magnitudes worth knowing when reasoning about this pipeline:

- A **full layout pass** on a moderately complex page: low single-digit milliseconds to tens of milliseconds, depending on tree size — expensive enough that doing it 60 times a second (once per animation frame) is a real budget constraint, not free.
- A **compositor-only frame** (pure `transform`/`opacity` change): often under 1ms of main-thread work, which is why it can hit 60fps even while other JS is running.
- **Critical CSS inlining**: commonly cited FCP improvements of 200-500ms on 3G-class connections, purely from removing one network round trip from the blocking path.
- **Layer memory**: each composited layer is a full bitmap at its rendered size — a handful of full-viewport `will-change` layers on a high-DPI mobile screen can add tens of megabytes of GPU memory, a real constraint on lower-end devices.

These numbers are what let you say "this will help" instead of "this should help" in a performance conversation.

slides.sectionTitle: Answering "how would you speed up first paint"
slides.markdown:
A structured answer walks the pipeline and names the blocker at each stage, rather than listing generic tips:

1. **Is a large stylesheet render-blocking above-the-fold content?** → inline critical CSS, async-load the rest.
2. **Is a synchronous script halting parsing before the render tree can be built?** → `defer`, or move it after content.
3. **Is layout itself expensive** (large DOM, complex flex/grid nesting)? → simplify the tree, or avoid layout thrashing (see `dom-and-cssom`).
4. **Is paint expensive** (many shadows, gradients, or a huge repainted area)? → check DevTools paint flashing, reduce the area or the effect count.
5. **Are animations forcing layout instead of compositing?** → switch to `transform`/`opacity`.

Naming which of these five is actually the bottleneck — with a DevTools Performance trace to back it up — is what distinguishes a senior answer from a list of best practices recited without evidence that any of them apply to this specific page.
